column1: What is the core architectural model of a hardware sequencer, invariant across all topologies?
column2: A circular buffer with programmable read logic: a clock-driven address pointer traverses stored CV/trigger data, and stateless output conversion turns each buffer position into analog voltages and gate pulses.

column1: Why can't a hardware sequencer generate its own independent timing reference in a modular patch?
column2: Because every module must stay phase-coherent with a single master clock; an independent internal clock would drift relative to other modules' LFOs, envelopes, and dividers, causing rhythmic instability.

column1: What two output-timing invariants must a hardware sequencer guarantee on each clock edge?
column2: 1) Clock-edge-to-CV-update latency must be deterministic and bounded (no jitter); 2) Gate outputs must transition before CV outputs settle, so envelopes don't retrigger against a still-changing pitch/filter CV.

column1: What distinguishes a MIDI status byte from a data byte at the bit level, and why does this matter?
column2: Status bytes have MSB=1; data bytes have MSB=0. This lets receivers resynchronize on status bytes after transmission errors, providing fault tolerance in MIDI's serial protocol.

column1: What is MIDI's serial transmission rate, and what structural limit does every MIDI message obey?
column2: 31.25 kilobaud; every message is a status byte followed by zero to two data bytes, never more.

column1: What is MIDI Clock's PPQN resolution, and what is the core tradeoff this creates?
column2: 24 pulses per quarter note (PPQN). This coarse resolution versus a sequencer's internal 960/1920 PPQN creates quantization error: events between ticks must shift to the nearest tick, introducing accumulating sub-millisecond timing jitter.

column1: What is the defining voltage standard of 1V/Octave CV pitch control, and what does 1 volt of change do?
column2: 1V/Oct is a logarithmic pitch scale where each 1V increase doubles the oscillator's output frequency (one octave up), mirroring equal-tempered tuning's 2:1 octave ratio.

column1: How many millivolts correspond to one semitone in the 1V/Octave standard, and how is this derived?
column2: Approximately 83.33 mV per semitone, derived by dividing 1 volt by 12 semitones per octave.

column1: What circuit function performs the 1V/Oct exponential pitch conversion inside an analog VCO, and name example ICs?
column2: An exponential voltage-to-current converter (matched transistor pairs or ICs like CEM3340/AS3340, SSM2210, V2164) converts linear control voltage into exponentially scaled current that charges timing capacitors to set oscillator frequency.

column1: What octave-tracking accuracy defines a well-calibrated modular oscillator, versus a poorly calibrated one?
column2: Well-calibrated: within ±5 cents across a five-octave range. Poorly calibrated/cheap designs: 10–20 cents drift in upper registers, causing audibly sour unison intervals.

column1: What is the PPQN resolution of Roland's DIN Sync protocol, and what temporal resolution does it yield?
column2: 24 pulses per quarter note, yielding 1/96th-note resolution—sufficient for straight sixteenths but marginal for triplets and swing quantization.

column1: Why is Eurorack clock synchronization ambiguous compared to MIDI Clock or DIN Sync?
column2: Eurorack uses simple analog rising-edge gate pulses (typically 5V) with no universal PPQN standard—different manufacturers implement varying pulse-per-quarter-note rates, unlike MIDI/DIN Sync's fixed 24 PPQN.
